zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription follows the supplied BnF scan; lexical data do not determine damaged glyphs.

lines.note: Catana completes Sorazaya from the preceding page. Sorazayamo naifito begins an idiomatic description of a person; the literal scabbard image should not be forced onto the figurative gloss that follows.

runs.text: ſingelo, & ſẽ dobrez. ¶ Itẽ, Homẽ apreſado

lines.note: The phrase first means a straightforward person without duplicity, then introduces an alternative sense of a hurried person. The scan has the nasal abbreviation ſẽ and the editorial Itẽ, not provisional ltẽ.

runs.text: & ſofrego ẽ tudo, & q̃ não da lugar, ou vagar

lines.note: Continues the hurried-person sense: eager in everything and allowing no time or leisure. Pera nada completes this sentence at the far right of the next row.

Sore is the demonstrative equivalent of that or that one. The right-hand (pera nada. finishes the preceding entry's Portuguese sentence; its displacement is preserved, while Sore is restored to upright headword type and the normal entry margin.
Sore gives a verb for a hawk or falcon escaping. It is distinct from the identically spelled demonstrative immediately above.
Sorearuqi denotes wandering away or avoiding company, as the continuing Portuguese explains. The historical principal forms are retained rather than normalized.

runs.text: decà peralà da conuerſação, & trato dos ho-

lines.note: The person wanders away from conversation and human company. The divided word is ho-mens; the first letter has the h form, not provisional b.
Mens completes homens and the reference to social dealings. The short continuation is retained as its own physical row.

runs.text: Falta, ou deſcuido q̃ hũ co-

lines.note: Soreacu, alternatively ſoriacu, is a fault or deliberate neglect toward someone. The headword's e is visible in the scan, correcting Sorcacu; co- begins comete below.

runs.text: mete de propoſito contra alguem. Vt,

lines.note: Mete completes comete: the fault is committed deliberately against someone. Fitoni begins the Japanese example of neglect toward a person.
Fitoni ſoriacu ſuru means failing in one's obligations toward someone. The Portuguese para-construction remains in its printed form pera cõ.

runs.text: Eu: palaura de que vſa ordinaria-

lines.note: Soregaxi is a first-person expression. The gloss begins Eu: rather than the provisional Eur, then explains who normally uses it.
Mente completes ordinariamente; the expression is used by dignified or respected people. The word space before gẽte is restored without expanding its nasal abbreviation.
Unmarked Sorei describes something light or of little substance. It must be kept separate from the following marked-vowel funeral term.
Sǒrei means burial or funeral observance. Both the marked headword and the example Sǒreiuo itaſu are visible; the missing accent and i in the provisional text are restored.
Sǒreiuo tori itonamu means arranging or conducting the funeral. The example repeats the rei component, including the i omitted by the provisional text.
Aparelhar o enterramento completes the explanation of preparing a funeral. It is the continuation of the preceding Japanese example.
Soreniyotte means for that reason or therefore, matching Por ißo. The attached Japanese components retain their printed spacing.
Soreſama is a respectful second-person expression, glossed as your honor. The scan supports Soreſama and Voſſa merce, not provisional Soroſama and Veſſa nerce.

runs.text: Eſſe eſſe, ou iſſo iſſo, ou aßi aßi.

lines.note: Soreſore is repeated demonstrative language: that one, that, or so. The first Portuguese demonstrative contains the repeated s-types, matching the following eſſe rather than the single-s provisional form.

runs.text: Cada hum, ou de cada hum.

lines.note: Soreſoreno has the distributive sense each or of each. The first component reads Sore-, not the provisional Soro-.
Soretçura means of that kind or sort. The final S. marks written usage and is upright in the scan.
Soretçure is given as another form with the same meaning. Idem refers back to the preceding entry rather than supplying a new gloss.
Sori here is bending or arching upward. It is the intransitive counterpart of the bodily-bending sense seen on the preceding page.
Ma completes cima. Nocqeni ſoru begins an example of arching backward, with the head position explained below.

runs.text: a cabeça hum pouco virada pera tras. ¶

lines.note: The head is turned somewhat backward. Ita introduces a further example, involving a board, which continues on the following row.
Ita, l, qiga ſoru describes a board or stick warping. The Latin alternative marker l is distinct from the Japanese qiga.
A second Sori entry means shaving. Camiuo ſo-ru exemplifies shaving the head and is physically divided here.
Ru completes ſoru; Rapar a cabeça supplies the complete translation. This is a continuation of the shaving sense, not of the preceding bending sense.
Soriacu is neglect, with a direct cross-reference to Soreacu earlier in the column. The referenced name visibly contains e, confirming the correction in that earlier headword.
Soricoboxi describes shaving while scattering the cut hair. The -oita principal form is retained as printed historical morphology.

runs.text: cabelos, ou botar os cabelos pera baixo.

lines.note: Completes the description of scattering hair or making it fall downward. It is the result of shaving, not an independent hair-related entry.

runs.text: Soricudaxi, ſu, aita. i, Sori voroſu.

lines.note: Soricudaxi, paraphrased as Sori voroſu, has the same shaving-downward sense. Idem links it to the preceding entry rather than defining a different action.
Sorifaxi is an arched bridge. The Portuguese adjective reads arcada, not the provisional arcoda; the Japanese faxi is the historical spelling of the bridge component.

Sôrin is first explained as vegetation or woodland, then given a religious sense below. The faint mark over the headword's first vowel is read as a circumflex; the following Sôrinzô supplies a local comparison.

runs.text: Tera dos Ienxùs. Aliquando os meſmos Ienxùs.

lines.note: The religious sense is a temple of the Ienxùs, or sometimes the monks themselves. Both occurrences retain the visible ù, correcting provisional Ienxis in the first. Tera and Ienxùs are Japanese terms embedded in Portuguese; the whole line is printed italic.
Sôrinzô denotes monks of the Ienxù group. The sect name is an embedded Japanese term within the italic Portuguese gloss, not an ordinary headword; its visible vowel mark is kept as ù.
Sôriǒ is the principal heir. The paired expression Sôriǒ ſoxi is explained below as the heir and a son who is not the heir; the Portuguese grave in Mòrgado is retained.

runs.text: mòrgado, & o que não he mòrgado.

lines.note: Completes the paired example as an heir and a non-heir. The first word is mòrgado, not provisional mirgado, and the printed accents are preserved.

Sôriǒxiqi denotes the heirship or inheritance. The headword is abraded; its longer riǒ sequence is preferred to provisional ro, with the vowel marks remaining a nonblocking uncertainty. The supplied NINJAL index corroborates the lexical identification but does not determine this copy's damaged accents.
Sorivoroxi is shaving and letting the hair fall downward. The principal form reads oita without a caron, correcting the provisional ǒita.
Baixo os cabelos completes the explanation of letting shaved hair fall below. The separate continuation is retained.
Sorivotoxi is another equivalent shaving verb. Camiuo begins the illustrative object phrase, with the verb following on the next row.
Camiuo ſorivotoſu is glossed as shaving so that the hair falls down. The example preserves the printed compound and attached object particle.
Em baixo completes the direction in the preceding translation. It remains a short physical body line rather than being merged upward.

Soro, alternatively ſorǒ, is described as a substantive verb meaning to be. Verb. is legible; the last letter of the abraded abbreviation Subſtãt. is a context-supported t reading and remains uncertain. No additional first-vowel accent is imported from lexical normalization.
The entry adds that the same form can sometimes function as a particle. Aliquando is the printed Latin adverb, correcting the provisional extra vowel.

runs.text: ſe ajunta aos verbos na eſcriptura ſẽ ſentido.

lines.note: The particle is attached to verbs in writing without an independent meaning. The restored sentence reads ajunta and eſcriptura; ſẽ remains abbreviated rather than expanded to sem.
Sǒro is dew on grass or herbs, directly paraphrased by Cuſano tçuyu. The scan has a caron and initial O in Orualho, not provisional Sôro and Crualho; the entry begins at the normal headword margin.
Sǒrǒ is sea waves, paraphrased by Auoi nami. Both vowel marks are retained as carons, and S. is the upright written-register label.
A separate Sǒro denotes frost and dew. Ximo here means frost in the Japanese paraphrase and is not the geographical name used elsewhere.

runs.text: Taboinha com contas ẽfiadas em a-

lines.note: Soroban is an abacus described as a small board with beads strung on wire. The first vowel of ẽfiadas carries the nasal abbreviation omitted in the provisional transcription.

runs.text: rame por onde contão os Chinas, & Iapoẽs.

lines.note: Rame completes arame, the wire on which the beads are threaded. The gloss identifies Chinese and Japanese users; the tilde in Iapoẽs is retained over its printed vowel.
Sorobiqi means trailing or dragging a garment or similar object. Veſti- begins vestido and continues below.
Do completes vestido, dragged along the ground. Qitçunega vouo ſoro-biqu begins the example of a fox trailing its tail; the final mark is a hyphen rather than the provisional period.

runs.text: A rapoſa arroja o rabo pollo chão.

lines.note: Biqu completes the fox example; the Portuguese states that the fox drags its tail along the ground. Vouo belongs to the tail plus object particle, not a separate verb.
Soroi means to come together or agree. The circumflexes in rô and ôta are visible in the principal forms and are not replaced by carons.
Fiǒxiga ſorôte vomoxiroi describes musical rhythms or parts agreeing pleasingly. The Portuguese begins an explanation of their concordance across the next rows.

runs.text: dando as vozes da muſica, & dos inſtrumẽtos

lines.note: The voices in the music and the instruments are coordinated. Inſtrumẽtos keeps its nasal abbreviation rather than silently expanding it.

runs.text: em hum compaßo he pera ouuir. ¶

lines.note: The coordinated music is worth hearing in one measure or beat. Fiǒ begins the contrasting compound continued as xiga below. Enlarged comparison shows a round terminal mark, transcribed as a full stop rather than inventing a hyphen from the word continuation; the Japanese letters are upright, not mixed with the italic gloss.
Xiga ſorouanu completes the negative example, meaning the musical parts do not agree. Vo- begins vozes in the continuing Portuguese translation.

Zes completes vozes. Cocoroga ſoro followed by uanu below expresses disagreement of hearts or intentions. The visible round terminal mark is retained as a full stop despite the continuing verb; physical punctuation is not normalized to an expected hyphen.
Uanu completes the negative verb. The translation speaks of hearts and, on the next row, wills not agreeing.
Vontades completes the reference to differing wills or intentions. The short physical continuation belongs to the concordance entry.
Sôron is dispute or contention, with Ai, ronzuru as the Japanese paraphrase. The scan reads Diſputa and the complete conjunction ou, correcting both provisional omissions.

Contenda completes Sôron. The right-hand (pouco. is displaced material completing pouco a pouco in the next entry; it was omitted from the provisional text and is restored at its actual physical position.
Sororiſororito is an adverb meaning slowly or little by little. The final pouco of the Portuguese phrase is physically above, at the right end of the preceding row.
Sororito is a shorter equivalent adverb. Idem refers to the slow or gradual manner described immediately above.
Soroſoroto is another adverb with the same meaning. Adu. and Idem are italic grammatical and editorial apparatus.
Soroye means assembling or making things equal. Cou- starts cousa, specifying objects of the same kind below.
Sa completes cousa. Yaſaqiuo ſoroyuru means aligning arrowheads; the verb is printed continuously, without the provisional space in ſoro yuru.

runs.text: Ajũtar, ou igualar as pontas das frechas como

lines.note: The Portuguese explains joining or aligning arrowheads. The following row supplies the context of multiple people shooting together.
Completes the coordinated-arrow example. Cuchi- begins a new example whose object particle uo is carried onto the following physical row.
Cuchiuo ſoroyete mǒſu means all speaking with one voice. The division Cuchi-uo remains physical rather than being rewritten into a modern word division.
Boca completes speaking with one mouth or in the same way. Focono starts another example, referring to spear points on the next row.
Focono ſaqiuo ſoroyuru concerns aligning spear points. The Portuguese has the nasal abbreviation lãças, restoring the omitted tilde rather than expanding it to lanças.

runs.text: juntas a piq̃, ou a ponto. ¶

lines.note: The spears are together and ready. Xeiuo ſoroyuru introduces assembling military forces; the verb begins with long ſ, not the provisional f, and the punctuation after piq̃ is retained.

runs.text: Ajuntar, ou fazer gente de guerra.

lines.note: The example means gathering or raising soldiers. Gente de guerra supplies the sense of Japanese Xei without requiring a modernized transcription.

runs.text: Comer großeiro, mal feito, & ſem ſa-

lines.note: Soſai denotes coarse, badly prepared and tasteless food. Sa-bor is physically divided between this row and the next.
Bor completes sabor. Soſaina teide gozaru begins a host's self-deprecating remark about the food, explained in the following lines.

runs.text: que diz o que conuida a alguem humilhandoſe

lines.note: Explains that the host says this when inviting someone to eat, humbling himself. The reflexive humilhandoſe belongs to the Portuguese explanation, not to the Japanese utterance.

runs.text: que he hũa maneira de comer aquelle mal feito,

lines.note: The guest is being offered a supposedly poorly made meal. The nasal abbreviation hũa and the demonstrative aquelle are retained rather than modernized.
Großeiro completes the host's self-deprecating description of the food as coarse. This is the end of the first Soſai entry, not the beginning of the next sense.

runs.text: Soſai. i, Arai coto, comai coto.

lines.note: The second Soſai contrasts Arai coto with comai coto, coarse and fine matters. Groſ- begins the first Portuguese adjective and is completed on the next physical row.
Completes grossa and contrasts it with fine or minute things. The example reads ſaini, not the provisional ſami; it contrasts coarse and fine detail and continues i-ru below.
Ru completes the Japanese verb iru. The Portuguese means understanding and engaging thoroughly with broad matters as well as details; the scan supports Entẽder and groſſo, not Enteder and graſſo.

runs.text: no miudo. ¶ Item, Em couſas de eſtudo, &

lines.note: Finishes the broad-and-fine distinction and introduces an application to study and learning. The paragraph mark and Item separate an additional explanatory sense within the same entry.

runs.text: letras eſtar viſto ẽ tudo, aßino ſuperficial como

lines.note: Describes being versed in every aspect of learning, both superficial and detailed. The printed nasal abbreviation ẽ and joined aßino are retained without editorial expansion or spacing normalization.
The explanation ends with minute and profound matters. Soſaina begins a new adjectival example whose noun fito is on the following physical row.

runs.text: Homem muito miudo, & que em tudo

lines.note: Fito completes Soſaina fito, a person attentive to detail and knowledgeable about everything. This is an indented continuation of the preceding example, not a separate headword.
Entende completes the description of the knowledgeable, meticulous person. The concluding &c. remains part of this definition.

runs.text: O vir, ou ir de preßa.

lines.note: Fayacu mairu identifies coming or going quickly. The headword is read Sǒſan rather than the provisional Sǒfan; the worn medial long-s form is interpreted with the Japanese phrase, while the printed Portuguese preßa is retained.
A separate homographic Sǒſan entry denotes silkworms. It must not be merged with the preceding verb-related entry merely because their headings agree.
Sǒſǒ and Fayǒ mean quickly. The Portuguese has Depreßa without the extra provisional ſ; mǒxi- begins the example verb continued below.

runs.text: Logo de preßa mãdarei, ou da-

lines.note: Tçuqeôzu completes mǒxitçuqeôzu, promising to order or arrange something promptly. The visible terminal hyphen in da- is restored; rei on the next row completes darei.

Rei completes darei ordem, 'I shall give instructions.' The last letter is i, not the provisional t. The worn right-hand Sǒsǒ is a separate catchword for the next page, assigned to furniture rather than this body line.

The catchword is abraded, especially its medial s and vowel marks. Sǒsǒ is the usable chosen reading supported by the surviving shapes and the first heading on f449; no terminal period is supplied where none is secure.
